strengths: PixelDiT offers a technically coherent and useful architecture for autoencoder-free image generation. A coarse semantic pathway conditions narrow pixel features through pixel-wise AdaLN, while compress–attend–expand operations provide global communication without full-resolution attention. The residual pixel pathway makes this meaningfully different from a mandatory autoencoder bottleneck.

ImageNet results provide strong empirical support: 1.61 FID and 0.64 recall at 320 epochs improve over the reported PixelFlow and PixNerd results. The reported 311 GFLOPs per forward pass also represents a favorable quality–compute tradeoff. The contribution remains valuable despite stronger results from some other generators.

The architectural ablations substantiate important design choices. At 80 epochs, pixel-wise modulation improves FID from 3.50 to 2.36; removing pixel-pathway attention worsens FID from 2.36 to 2.56, and from 1.97 to 2.22 at 160 epochs. Additional studies examine patch size, model scale, depth allocation, compaction rate, and sampling.

The text-to-image extension demonstrates practical scalability beyond ImageNet: the 1.3B model achieves 0.74 GenEval and 83.5 DPG-Bench at 1024 resolution. The qualitative samples support its ability to synthesize varied, detailed images. Architecture diagrams and supplementary optimization and guidance settings make the core method reasonably clear.
weaknesses: The broad claim of surpassing existing pixel generators is overstated. Section 4.2 and Table 11 acknowledge SiD2's better 1.38 FID, yet it is omitted from the principal comparison table because some metadata are unavailable. PixelDiT demonstrates a compelling efficiency–quality tradeoff, rather than unqualified pixel-space quality superiority.

The evidence supports this particular architecture more strongly than the claim that explicit pixel-token modeling is essential. Table 4 lacks parameter- or compute-matched controls for the substantially larger modulation projection, and the training recipe includes DINOv2 representation alignment without an ablation of its contribution. Table 5 also shows that the version without pixel-pathway attention remains strong. These results do not isolate pixel interactions as the main cause of the gains over other approaches.

Text-to-image reproducibility and attribution are limited by the description of the 26M training pairs: sources, filtering, caption construction, and benchmark-overlap controls are not specified. The exact Gemma-2 variant and system prompt are also unspecified. Consequently, the benchmark advantage cannot be cleanly attributed to the architecture rather than differences in training data and text conditioning.

Efficiency comparisons are incompletely controlled. Table 3 specifies GPU and precision but not throughput batch size, baseline sampling budgets, or whether text encoding and VAE decoding are included. Per-forward FLOPs in Table 11 do not establish end-to-end sampling efficiency, particularly since the best ImageNet result uses 100 steps. Training convergence is shown against iterations rather than measured compute or wall-clock time.

The claimed editing and fine-detail preservation advantages rely on a single bicycle-to-motorcycle example, without aggregate background-preservation or edit-success measurements. Avoiding VAE reconstruction loss is a valid motivation, but it does not guarantee preservation through denoising; similarly, residual connections do not prove that compaction never compromises detail. These claims should be narrower. Overall, these reservations limit the interpretation of the results but do not outweigh the supported architectural and empirical contribution.

strengths: The paper makes a useful architectural contribution: coarse semantic processing conditions a narrow pixel stream through pixel-wise modulation, while compress–attend–expand operations make global interaction affordable. The residual pixel pathway provides a technically plausible way to avoid an external autoencoder bottleneck.

ImageNet results are strong: PixelDiT-XL achieves 1.61 FID and 0.64 recall at 320 epochs, compared with 1.98/0.60 for PixelFlow and 1.93/0.60 for PixNerd (Table 1). Its reported 311 GFLOPs per forward pass provide a compelling quality–compute trade-off among pixel-space models.

The ablations substantiate the proposed design. Pixel-wise rather than patch-wise modulation improves FID from 3.50 to 2.36 at 80 epochs (Table 4). Removing pixel-pathway attention worsens FID from 1.97 to 2.22 at 160 epochs (Table 5). Additional studies examine patch size, model capacity, depth allocation, compaction rate, and sampling.

The extension to megapixel text-to-image generation is substantial evidence of practical usefulness. The 1.3B model achieves 0.74 GenEval and 83.5 DPG-Bench at 1024 resolution, accompanied by convincing qualitative examples. Together with the ImageNet experiments, this supports weak acceptance despite the reservations below.
weaknesses: The headline claim of surpassing existing pixel generators is overstated. Section 4.2 and Table 11 acknowledge SiD2's better 1.38 FID, but Table 1 excludes it because some metadata are unavailable, despite including other incompletely specified baselines. PixelDiT supports a strong efficiency–quality trade-off, not unqualified pixel-space quality leadership.

The broader claim that explicit pixel-token modeling is essential is not established. The main baseline is a patch-only velocity-prediction DiT; the paper itself describes JiT's alternative clean-image prediction approach. There is no controlled comparison separating architecture from prediction objective, nor an ablation of the pretrained DINOv2 alignment objective. The experiments demonstrate benefits under the chosen recipe rather than a general necessity.

Efficiency evidence is incomplete. Table 11 measures individual forward passes, whereas ImageNet results use 100 sampling steps; Appendix B.2 reports approximately 2.50 FID with 25 steps. Table 3 specifies an A100 and precision but does not sufficiently document throughput batch sizes, baseline sampling budgets, or inclusion of text encoding and decoding. Training-time and memory comparisons are also absent, limiting claims of faster convergence in computational terms.

Text-to-image reproducibility and attribution are limited by the description of the approximately 26M training pairs: sources, filtering, and caption preparation are unspecified. The Gemma-2 variant and actual system prompt are also unclear. Consequently, benchmark improvements over differently trained systems cannot be attributed cleanly to the architecture, although the experiments do demonstrate feasibility.

The editing advantage rests on one illustrated example in Figure 1(b), without aggregate preservation and edit-success measurements. VAE reconstructions support the proposed failure mechanism in that example, but do not establish generally superior editing. Likewise, residual connections permit detail preservation but do not prove the categorical claim that compaction cannot compromise fine details.

strengths: PixelDiT offers a technically coherent and useful architecture for direct pixel-space generation. Coarse semantic processing, pixel-specific AdaLN, and compress–attend–expand operations with pixel-level residual connections provide a practical way to combine global context with inexpensive per-pixel updates.

ImageNet results are strong: PixelDiT-XL achieves 1.61 FID and 0.64 recall at 320 epochs, compared with 1.98/0.60 for PixelFlow and 1.93/0.60 for PixNerd (Table 1). The reported 311 GFLOPs per forward pass also represents a favorable quality–compute trade-off against several pixel-space alternatives (Table 11).

The ablations provide meaningful architectural evidence. Pixel-wise conditioning improves FID from 3.50 to 2.36 at 80 epochs (Table 4), while removing pixel-pathway attention worsens FID at both 80 and 160 epochs (Table 5). Additional studies examine patch size, pathway depth, compaction rate, guidance, and sampling steps.

The extension to megapixel text-to-image generation substantially strengthens the contribution beyond ImageNet. The 1.3B model achieves 0.74 GenEval and 83.5 DPG at 1024 resolution, with convincing qualitative examples. Taken together, the demonstrated architecture and results support weak acceptance despite the reservations below.
weaknesses: The broad claim of surpassing existing pixel generators is overstated. The manuscript itself reports SiD2 at 1.38 FID, better than PixelDiT's 1.61. Missing parameter or training information does not justify omitting its known FID from the main comparison, especially when other rows contain missing fields. Table 11 appropriately reveals a more nuanced quality–compute trade-off. PixNerd's FID also differs between Tables 1 and 11 (1.93 versus 2.15) without explanation.

The experiments establish that the proposed design works, but less firmly establish the claimed necessity or uniqueness of its mechanism. Table 4 does not explicitly document whether REPA, optimization, guidance, and parameter budgets are matched across every variant, and no REPA ablation is provided. Table 5 supports a benefit from compact attention, rather than its necessity: the attention-free variant remains competitive at 2.56 versus 2.36 FID. Architectural distinctions from closely related semantic/detail designs and PixNerd could be sharper.

Text-to-image reproducibility is materially limited by the unspecified sources, filtering, and captioning of the approximately 26M training pairs. The exact Gemma-2 variant and system prompt are also unspecified. Consequently, the benchmark comparisons demonstrate system-level capability but do not isolate architectural gains from data and conditioning differences.

Efficiency evidence is useful but incomplete. Per-forward FLOPs and epoch counts do not establish total training efficiency, particularly with DINOv2 alignment. Table 3 identifies hardware and precision but omits throughput batch sizes, baseline sampling budgets, and whether text encoding and decoding are included. These omissions limit interpretation of the claimed speed advantages.

The detail-preservation claim rests on one editing example, without quantitative background-preservation or edit-success evaluation. It illustrates VAE reconstruction damage but cannot establish general editing superiority across different pretrained systems. Likewise, residual connections provide a route around compaction but do not guarantee that fine details are preserved. GenEval and DPG primarily assess alignment, leaving the broader high-frequency fidelity claim weakly measured.

strengths: PixelDiT provides a useful, technically coherent architecture for pixel-space generation. Pixel-wise semantic modulation and compress–attend–expand operations combine global communication with inexpensive per-pixel processing, while residual connections bypass the attention bottleneck.

The ImageNet results support a strong quality–compute trade-off: 1.61 FID at 256×256 with 311 GFLOPs per forward pass and 1.81 FID at 512×512. The 256×256 result improves on the reported PixelFlow, PixNerd, EPG, and JiT baselines, with competitive diversity.

Substantial ablations support the architectural choices. Pixel-wise modulation improves FID from 3.50 to 2.36 at 80 epochs; removing pixel-pathway attention worsens FID from 1.97 to 2.22 at 160 epochs. Additional studies examine depth allocation, compaction rate, patch size, representation alignment, sampling, and longer training.

The extension to megapixel text-to-image generation is convincing evidence of practical scalability: the 1.3B model achieves 0.74 GenEval and 83.5 DPG-Bench at 1024 resolution. The appendix also evaluates background preservation on 281 editing pairs, extending the evidence beyond selected examples. Together, these supported contributions favor acceptance despite the reservations below.
weaknesses: The broad claim of surpassing existing pixel-space generators is inaccurate. Section 4.2 acknowledges SiD2's 1.38 FID at 256×256, and Table 15 reports it explicitly, versus PixelDiT's 1.61. Missing training metadata does not justify excluding a stronger result from the main quality comparison, particularly when other included methods also have missing metadata. PixelDiT's favorable compute trade-off is the better-supported claim.

The evidence does not fully isolate the proposed architecture as the principal reason pixel-space training becomes practical. REPA has a large effect: removing it worsens 80-epoch FID from 2.36 to 6.58, and Appendix G reports eventual divergence without alignment. The method therefore depends materially on pretrained semantic supervision. Table 5 also lacks parameter/compute accounting across variants, limiting attribution of improvements specifically to the proposed mechanisms.

Efficiency comparisons are incomplete. Forward-pass FLOPs exclude training-time alignment overhead, and convergence by epochs does not establish wall-clock or total-compute efficiency. Text-to-image throughput specifies hardware and precision but not sufficiently detailed baseline sampling and batching protocols. These omissions weaken comparative efficiency claims without invalidating the reported generation quality.

The editing evaluation measures background preservation without measuring successful execution of the requested edit. Lower background MSE can accompany weaker edits, so Table 14 does not establish a superior preservation–editing trade-off. Likewise, residual bypasses make detail preservation plausible but do not guarantee that learned compaction cannot compromise fine details.

Reproducibility is uneven despite detailed architecture and optimization tables. The 26M-pair text-to-image dataset lacks sources and a reproducible collection/filtering recipe; exact Gemma-2 and DINOv2 variants and ImageNet logit-normal parameters are unspecified. These gaps particularly limit independent reproduction of the text-to-image results.

strengths: PixelDiT provides a useful architectural contribution to pixel-space generation: a coarse semantic transformer conditions a narrow pixel pathway through pixel-wise modulation, while compress–attend–expand operations make global communication affordable. The design is technically coherent, although its building blocks draw on established methods.

The ImageNet results demonstrate a strong quality–compute trade-off. At 256×256, PixelDiT achieves FID 1.61 after 320 epochs with 311 GFLOPs per forward pass, compared with reported FIDs of 1.98 for PixelFlow and 1.93 for PixNerd. Results at 512×512 and megapixel text-to-image generation provide meaningful evidence that the architecture extends beyond one benchmark setting.

The ablations substantiate the main design choices. Table 5 improves FID from 8.53 for the augmented patch-only baseline to 3.50 with the dual pathway and compaction, then to 2.36 with pixel-wise AdaLN. Table 6 separately demonstrates a smaller but consistent benefit from pixel-pathway attention. Additional studies cover model size, depth allocation, compaction rate, REPA, guidance, and sampling.

The appendix strengthens the practical evidence: editing is evaluated on 281 pairs rather than only the introductory example, and architecture, optimization, sampling settings, and unsuccessful experiments are documented. Taken together, the supported architectural and empirical contributions favor acceptance despite the qualifications below.
weaknesses: The claim of surpassing existing pixel generators is overstated. Section 4.2 explicitly acknowledges SiD2's 1.38 FID at 256×256, and Table 15 includes it, whereas PixelDiT obtains 1.61. Missing metadata for SiD2 does not justify an unqualified state-of-the-art claim or its exclusion from the main comparison, especially when other rows contain missing fields. PixelDiT's defensible advantage is its quality–compute trade-off, not universally superior fidelity.

The attribution of success primarily to pixel modeling needs qualification. Table 11 shows that removing pretrained DINOv2 alignment worsens FID from 2.36 to 6.58 at 80 epochs; Section G.3 additionally reports instability and eventual divergence without alignment. This dependency does not invalidate the autoencoder-free architecture, but it materially limits claims about a self-contained training recipe. The main architectural ablation also lacks parameter- and compute-matched controls for the substantially larger pixel-wise modulation projection.

The efficiency evidence is stronger for forward-pass cost than for total training efficiency. Training epochs and single-pass GFLOPs do not account for the alignment encoder, optimization overhead, or differing sampling budgets. The 512×512 result requires 320 epochs of lower-resolution pretraining plus 530 epochs of fine-tuning. Table 4 specifies hardware and precision for throughput but omits sufficient baseline sampling and batching details to establish a controlled speed comparison.

The editing experiment measures background preservation without measuring whether the requested edits succeed across the dataset. Table 14's lower background MSE and higher SSIM are encouraging, but can also favor conservative edits. Consequently, the results do not establish superior editing quality at matched edit strength or isolate the VAE as the cause of the full performance difference. Likewise, residual connections preserve an information path but do not guarantee that token compaction cannot compromise fine detail.

Text-to-image reproducibility remains limited: the approximately 26M training pairs lack documented sources and curation procedures, and the exact Gemma-2 and DINOv2 variants are unspecified. Cross-system benchmark differences therefore cannot be attributed cleanly to architecture. A smaller presentation inconsistency is the claim of direct 1024-resolution pretraining, whereas the documented recipe starts at 512 and subsequently fine-tunes at 1024.

strengths: PixelDiT provides a technically plausible and useful architecture for direct pixel-space generation. Coarse semantic processing, pixel-specific modulation, and compress–attend–expand operations enable global interaction while retaining a full-resolution residual pathway. The contribution is a practical architectural advance, even though its constituent mechanisms build on established ideas.

ImageNet results are strong: 1.61 FID at 256×256 after 320 epochs and 1.81 at 512×512, with recall of 0.64 and 0.67 respectively. Table 15 reports 311 GFLOPs per forward pass, supporting an attractive quality–compute trade-off relative to several pixel-space alternatives.

The ablations provide substantial evidence for the design. Table 5 improves FID from 8.53 for the augmented patch-only baseline to 3.50 with the dual-level design and compaction, then to 2.36 with pixel-wise modulation. Additional experiments examine pixel-pathway attention, compaction rate, depth allocation, patch size, representation alignment, and sampling choices.

The extension to megapixel text-to-image generation demonstrates usefulness beyond ImageNet. The 1.3B-parameter model achieves 0.74 GenEval and 83.5 DPG, with convincing qualitative examples. The appendix also quantifies editing background preservation over 281 pairs rather than relying solely on the introductory example.

Architecture and optimization details are generally well documented, and the appendix candidly discusses unsuccessful designs and training instability. Overall, the supported architectural and empirical contribution favors acceptance despite the limitations below.
weaknesses: The broad claim of surpassing existing pixel generators is overstated. The manuscript itself reports SiD2 achieving 1.38 FID at 256×256, better than PixelDiT's 1.61. Missing ancillary statistics justify qualification, not exclusion from the main comparison. PixelDiT establishes a competitive quality–compute trade-off rather than universal superiority.

The editing evaluation measures preservation without measuring successful execution of the requested edit. Lower background MSE and higher SSIM can also reflect more conservative editing. Table 14 therefore supports background consistency, but does not establish superior editing performance at comparable edit strength or isolate the VAE as the sole cause of differences.

Reproducibility is materially weaker for text-to-image experiments. The approximately 26M training pairs lack sufficient information about sources, filtering, and caption construction; the exact Gemma-2 variant and system prompt are also unspecified. These factors can substantially affect GenEval and DPG, limiting attribution of cross-model differences to the architecture.

Efficiency evidence is stronger for inference FLOPs than for total training cost. Epoch counts across architectures and resolutions are not equivalent compute budgets; the 512×512 result requires 320 epochs of pretraining plus 530 fine-tuning epochs. REPA also adds a frozen encoder during training. Table 4 gives hardware and precision but insufficient batch-size and baseline sampling details to fully assess throughput comparisons.

Some mechanistic claims exceed the evidence. Residual connections provide a route around attention compression, but do not guarantee that compaction preserves fine details. Likewise, Table 6 shows a modest FID improvement from compact attention, not that it is necessary for practical generation. Table 11's large REPA benefit also shows that the successful recipe depends substantially on pretrained representation supervision, alongside the proposed pixel-modeling architecture.
